kilauea_notices.title: HAWAIIAN VOLCANO OBSERVATORY DAILY UPDATE
kilauea_notices.message: HVO Kilauea YELLOW/ADVISORY - The Halema'uma'u eruption of Kīlauea remains paused following episode 56 fountaining on November 5. The summit is reinflating and the episode 57 forecast window is November 17-22.
kilauea_notices.detail: Overview: The Kīlauea summit eruption within Halema'uma'u is currently paused after episode 56 fountaining ended on November 5. The summit has been steadily reinflating since the end of episode 56, but slowed slightly over the past day. Another fountaining episode remains likely and the current forecast window for episode 57 fountaining is November 17-22. Summit Observations: Summit webcams recorded moderate to strong glow from the southwest vent and moderate glow from the north vent overnight. During a helicopter overflight on November 10, USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory Scientists observed a roiling lava surface in both vents about 130-165 feet (40-50 meters) deep. Seismic tremor remains elevated during the eruption pause. One small earthquake was located at the summit in the past day. The Uēkahuna tiltmeter (UWD) has recorded continued summit inflation following the end of episode 56 lava fountaining, which slowed down slightly over the past day. This morning, UWD has recovered a total of about 11 microradians of inflationary tilt since the end of episode 56. The average sulfur dioxide (SO2) emission rate recorded by the summit gas monitoring array yesterday, November 12, was about 3,000 tonnes per day. Trade winds this morning are carrying volcanic gases to the southwest. Rift Zone Observations: Rates of seismicity and ground deformation remain low in the East Rift Zone and Southwest Rift Zone. SO2 emissions from the East Rift Zone remain below the detection limit. Analysis: Following the end of episode 56 on November 5, 2026, summit tiltmeters have recorded a typical post-fountaining recovery. The steady inflationary trend flattened out for several hours last night but continues to slowly inflate this morning. Based on previous episodes, the ongoing tilt trend, and glow within the eruptive vents, another fountaining episode is likely. The forecast window for episode 57 fountaining is November 17-22. Kīlauea has been erupting episodically since December 23, 2024, from two primary vents (north and south) within Halemaʻumaʻu at the summit. Lava fountaining episodes generally last less than 12 hours and are separated by pauses of two or more weeks. HVO continues to closely monitor Kīlauea and remains in contact with Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park and the Hawaiʻi County Civil Defense Agency regarding eruptive hazards. Summary of episode 56: Lava fountaining occurred between 12:10 p.m. and 6:01 p.m. on November 5, 2026. Maximum fountain heights were about 660 feet (200 meters). Only the north vent produced fountaining. Tephra fallout was primarily towards the southwest, in closed areas of Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park, with trace amounts on Highway 11. The eruptive plume rose as high as 18,000 feet (5,500 meters) above sea level. Tiltmeter data indicate approximately 8 million cubic yards (6 million cubic meters) of lava were erupted, with an average eruption rate of 260 cubic yards (200 cubic meters) per second. The Uēkahuna tiltmeter (UWD) recorded a total of 17 microradians of deflationary tilt. Hazards: Eruptive activity since December 2024 has been occurring within a closed area of Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park. However, recent intrusions highlight that the location of eruptive activity could change. Intrusions can also be hazardous with potential to cause earthquakes, ground cracks, and small landslides. The primary hazards at Kīlauea due to eruptive activity and/or intrusions are: Volcanic Gas: High levels of volcanic gas—primarily water vapor (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), and sulfur dioxide (SO2)—are continually released during an eruption. Emissions can remain locally hazardous in the areas immediately downwind of the vents, even when the vents are not actively erupting. SO2 reacts in the atmosphere to create vog (volcanic air pollution) downwind. SO2 and vog may cause respiratory and other problems at high concentrations. mauna_loa_notices.title: HAWAIIAN VOLCANO OBSERVATORY MONTHLY UPDATE
mauna_loa_notices.message: HVO Mauna Loa GREEN/NORMAL - Mauna Loa earthquake counts were within typical levels in October, and minor inflation continues.
mauna_loa_notices.detail: Mauna Loa had a slight increase in seismic activity compared to the previous month; a total of 66 earthquakes were detected in Mauna Loa's summit region during the October reporting period, after 53 in September. These variations are within the typical range for the past two years. Most earthquakes occurred deep beneath the upper Southwest Rift Zone or broadly scattered around the upper flanks. Data from Global Positioning System (GPS) instruments on Mauna Loa showed slight inflation across the summit region in the past month. Oscillations between contraction and inflation patterns during non-eruptive periods are normal, but inflation has been the dominant trend since the 2022 eruption, consistent with magma refilling the summit reservoir system. Gas and temperature data from a station on Mauna Loa's Southwest Rift Zone indicate these values are at background levels, with little change relative to previous months. HVO continues to closely monitor Mauna Loa and will issue another update in one month, or earlier, should conditions change significantly.
